title: Contract-to-hire vs. permanent hiring: When each model makes sense.
summary: Learn how contract-to-hire works, how it compares to permanent hiring on cost and risk, which roles suit each model, and when to run both.
body_markdown:
### Key takeaways:


- When someone is brought in on a “contract-to-hire” arrangement, it means the company has brought them on for a specific time period, usually three to six months, with the intention of moving them to a permanent role at the end. Companies generally fill contract-to-hire positions via a staffing partner.
- Contract-to-hire decisions are driven more often by budget approval than by uncertainty about the candidate. A contract clears in about a week; a permanent requisition can take three months of headcount justification and finance sign-off.
- Before opening a permanent requisition, ask whether you'll want this person doing this work two years from now. If the answer isn't clear, a contract is the lower-risk starting point.
- Security teams belong on permanent headcount because the knowledge compounds. Migrations and platform builds suit contractors because the work has a defined end state.
- Candidates often read a contract offer as a lesser opportunity. In most large organizations it reflects how procurement works, not how the company values the role.
- Conversion outcomes are set in the first conversation with the hiring leader. Establish whether the permanent role is real before anyone signs.


Most companies choose contract-to-hire for reasons that have little to do with their evaluation of the candidate. A contract budget clears in a week. A permanent requisition takes three months of headcount justification and finance sign-off. Hiring leaders with work sitting in front of them tend to use whichever channel moves.


I've spent 14 years in tech recruiting across Philadelphia, Chicago, and DC, running a full desk, which means I'm the same person talking to the hiring leader and the candidate on every engagement. When a contract-to-hire is structured as one from the first conversation, my team converts well over 90% of those people into permanent roles.


These arrangements account for a substantial share of how U.S. companies staff. Staffing firms employed


[9.5 million temporary and contract workers](https://americanstaffing.net/posts/2026/03/30/employment-and-sales-rebound-in-q4/) over the course of 2025. Below is how the model works, how it compares to permanent hiring on cost and risk, which roles suit each, and why most teams should run both.


## What contract-to-hire is and how it works.


Contract-to-hire is a hiring arrangement in which a company brings someone on through a staffing agency for a defined period, typically three to six months, with the stated intent of moving them into a permanent role at the end of it. The mechanics are consistent across most engagements:


- **During the contract.** The worker stays on the agency's payroll, and the agency covers wages, payroll taxes, unemployment insurance, and benefits while billing the employer an hourly rate.


- **At conversion.** The employer pays a conversion fee and moves the person onto its own payroll.


- **If the fit isn't there.** The assignment ends and the agency absorbs the offboarding.


That structure is why the model gets described as “try before you buy.” The description is accurate as far as the mechanics go, but it skips past the reason most of my clients reach for it.


### Why hiring leaders choose contract-to-hire.


Budgeting for a contract is easier than budgeting for a permanent requisition by a significant margin. Opening a permanent role at a large company means headcount justification, finance sign-off, and several layers of approval, and it can be months before anyone posts anything. Approving a contractor means moving money a hiring leader often already controls.


The play I see most often looks like this: a client calls needing a six-month contract-to-hire, interviews one or two people through me, and starts someone within weeks. Meanwhile, they begin the permanent requisition approval, knowing it will clear in roughly six months. When it clears, they already have a trained contractor in the seat.


## Contract-to-hire vs. permanent hiring at a glance.


The two models differ in who employs the worker, how quickly the role gets filled, and where the risk sits if the hire doesn't work out. Cost is where the comparison gets misread most often. An hourly bill rate looks expensive next to a salary, but the bill rate already carries costs that a permanent hire carries too. Benefits alone accounted for


[30.1% of total compensation for private industry workers](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/ecec.nr0.htm) in March 2026, and that's before payroll taxes, recruiting spend, or the cost of a role sitting open.

## When a permanent hire is worth the commitment.


My test is simple. If you can't say with confidence that you'll want this work done by this person two years from now, you're probably looking at a contract.


That bar is higher than it seems. Median tenure for workers ages 25 to 34 is


[3 years](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/tenure.nr0.htm) . Setting a two-year horizon asks the work to hold someone for most of the time they’re likely to stay with an employer. What makes the test useful is that it forces you to examine the work itself: whether the function or project still exists in two years, and whether it changes enough over that span to keep someone interested in staying.


The threshold sits that high because the exit costs are lopsided. Ending a contract means reaching an end date. Ending a permanent hire means performance management, severance exposure,


[COBRA](https://www.dol.gov/general/topic/health-plans/cobra) , unemployment claims, and then paying to recruit a replacement. The employer carries all of it, and none of it shows up in the salary figure that got the requisition approved in the first place.


When a role clears that test, permanent hiring is the right model. From there the difficulty moves to execution, because a direct placement search gets lost more often in scoping and speed than in sourcing.


## Which roles suit contract-to-hire, and which need permanent headcount.


Some functions fail the two-year test structurally. The work has an end state built into it, and hiring permanently produces turnover you could have predicted at the scoping stage.


The clearest case is a role whose purpose is to make itself unnecessary. A DevOps engineer arrives when deployments break, pipelines are manual, and systems go down at night. Eighteen months later deployments are clean, the pipeline runs itself, and nothing goes down. I watch those engineers leave at almost exactly that point. Nothing went wrong. They finished the interesting work, and no one had lined up what came next.


A few patterns hold across most of my clients:


- **Security belongs on permanent headcount.** A security team has to learn your architecture, your threat model, and your regulatory obligations, and that knowledge compounds every year someone stays. Institutional context is most of the job.


- **Migrations and platform builds are contract work.** A cloud migration has a defined end state. When a client tells me they want to staff one with permanent engineers, I ask what those people are doing the month after it finishes. Usually nobody has worked that out yet. Staff it with contractors, then decide at the end whether to convert a couple who understand the new environment best.


- **Infrastructure and QA depend on what's ahead of them.** A two-year build justifies permanent hires. Stabilization work with a foreseeable finish line doesn't, and treating it as permanent is how you end up with bored engineers auditing their own automation.


But the right model for a role can change as the work changes. A role that warranted a contractor during a migration can warrant permanent headcount a year later, and the reverse happens just as often. Before you open a requisition, run the two-year test against the work sitting in front of that role now, not the work that justified it when you first scoped it.


## Why contract-to-hire conversions succeed or fail.


The outcome is usually determined in the first conversation with the hiring leader, before anyone looks at a resume. A client who tells me that this is a real permanent need with a slow-moving requisition already knows they'll want the work done for years. A client who tells me not to call it a contract-to-hire, that there's budget and work but no certainty past that, is saying something different. Both are legitimate, but the distinction matters enormously to the person being asked to take the job.


Candidates sometimes read a contract offer as a lesser opportunity, but in most large organizations it reflects how procurement runs rather than how the company values the role. Saying that plainly is part of my job. What I won't do is let someone believe a permanent role is waiting when the hiring leader never said so. Trust is thin enough already, and an agency that spends it to close one placement costs its client the next five.


Once the contract starts, the failures I see have almost nothing to do with capability. The top reason new hires leave early, regardless of contract type, is mismatched expectations, followed by lack of connection. A manager tells me a contractor isn't taking initiative. I ask whether they've said so directly, and the answer is usually “not really.” In one case a contractor had spent weeks waiting to hear from a colleague who'd been reassigned without anyone mentioning it. Thirty minutes of direct conversation early on is the cheapest retention tool in the arrangement, and it's the one most often skipped.


## Choosing the model before you open the requisition.


The decision comes down to what you know about the work: how long it runs, whether it has an end state, and whether it changes enough to hold someone for two years. Most teams answer that once, at the beginning, and never revisit it as the roadmap moves.
